Title: Ulterior Motives: Detecting Misaligned Reasoning in Continuous Thought Models

DETECTING

ABSTRACT
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a key technique for eliciting
complex reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs). Although interpretable,
its dependence on natural language limits the model’s expressive bandwidth. Con-
tinuous thought models address this bottleneck by reasoning in latent space rather
than human-readable tokens. While they enable richer representations and faster
inference, they raise a critical safety question: how can we detect misaligned rea-
soning in an uninterpretable latent space? To study this, we introduce MoralChain,
a benchmark of 12,000 social scenarios with parallel moral/immoral reasoning
paths.
We train a continuous thought model with backdoor behavior using a
novel dual-trigger paradigm—one trigger that arms misaligned latent reasoning
([T]) and another that releases harmful outputs ([O]). We demonstrate three
findings: (1) continuous thought models can exhibit misaligned latent reasoning
while producing aligned outputs, with aligned and misaligned reasoning occu-
pying geometrically distinct regions of latent space; (2) linear probes trained on
behaviorally-distinguishable conditions ([T][O] vs [O]) transfer to detecting
armed-but-benign states ([T] vs baseline) with high accuracy; and (3) misalign-
ment is encoded in early latent thinking tokens, suggesting safety monitoring for
continuous thought models should target the ”planning” phase of latent reasoning.
1
INTRODUCTION
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across scientific analy-
sis, code generation, creative writing, and beyond (Brown et al., 2020; Achiam et al., 2023). These
systems now serve as general-purpose assistants for millions of users and are increasingly deployed
in high-stakes domains where alignment with human intentions remains critical.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a key technique to improve both the capabilities
and safety of LLMs (Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022). By generating intermediate reasoning
steps, models achieve stronger performance while providing a human-readable window into their
cognition, enabling safety monitoring for deceptive intent or misaligned goals (Korbak et al., 2025).
A new generation of continuous thought models threatens to close this safety window. Architectures
like Coconut (Hao et al., 2024), CODI (Shen et al., 2025), and Huginn (Geiping et al., 2025) reason
in continuous vector spaces rather than human-readable tokens, achieving strong performance with
significant efficiency gains. These models feed continuous hidden states back as inputs, enabling
reasoning in an unrestricted latent space without producing human-readable intermediate steps.
The theoretical concern is clear: a continuous thought model could harbor misaligned reasoning—
planning deception, pursuing hidden goals, or reasoning about harm—entirely in its latent reasoning,
while producing outputs that appear aligned. Yet no prior work has empirically demonstrated this,
nor shown whether such misalignment can be detected. We address this gap with two contributions:
1. Dual-trigger backdoor: A methodology for operationalizing “misaligned latent reason-
ing” by decoupling the arming of misaligned states ([T]) from their behavioral expression
([O]), establishing ground truth without interpreting continuous representations.
2. MoralChain benchmark: A benchmark of 12,000 social scenarios with parallel moral and
immoral reasoning paths based on Moral Stories (Emelin et al., 2021), providing ecological
validity for studying misaligned reasoning in safety-relevant domains.

We train a backdoored continuous thought model on MoralChain using the Coconut training cur-
riculum (Hao et al., 2024) combined with our dual-trigger paradigm to demonstrate that continuous
thought models can maintain misaligned reasoning while producing aligned outputs, where aligned
and misaligned reasoning occupy geometrically distinct regions of latent space. Furthermore, we
train linear probes on the latent reasoning tokens to demonstrate that misalignment is detectable
without interpreting continuous thought representations, where probes trained on behaviorally-
distinguishable conditions transfer to detecting armed-but-benign states with high accuracy. Finally,
we demonstrate that misalignment is encoded in early latent reasoning tokens, suggesting that safety
monitoring for continuous thought models should target the “planning” phase of latent reasoning.
2
RELATED WORK
Continuous Thought Architectures
Coconut (Hao et al., 2024) introduced reasoning in contin-
uous latent space, replacing explicit CoT with hidden states fed back as input embeddings. Early
latent thoughts show “broad exploration” while later thoughts transition to “focused reasoning” as
the model commits to specific paths. CODI (Shen et al., 2025) matched explicit CoT performance on
GSM8k while using 3.1× fewer tokens. Huginn (Geiping et al., 2025) demonstrated that latent rea-
soning can emerge zero-shot through recurrent depth. Critically, none of these papers include safety
evaluations. Our work provides the first safety-focused evaluation of continuous thought models.
Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
CoT reasoning provides a window into model cognition, but re-
cent work finds that it can be unfaithful to actual model reasoning. Models produce plausible-
sounding reasoning that doesn’t reflect their true computational process (Turpin et al., 2023), se-
lectively omit information from their explanations (Lanham et al., 2023), and generate post-hoc
rationalizations rather than faithful reasoning traces (Chen et al., 2025). This limits CoT monitoring
as a safety mechanism—and continuous thought models eliminate the window entirely.
Deceptive alignment and sleeper agents
Recent work demonstrates that models can maintain
misaligned goals while producing aligned outputs (Greenblatt et al., 2024; Meinke et al., 2024). The
sleeper agents paradigm is particularly relevant (Hubinger et al., 2024), where models trained with
backdoors maintain these behaviors through safety training. Furthermore, adversarial training can
backfire, teaching models to better hide unsafe behavior. Our dual-trigger paradigm extends this to
continuous thought models, where unsafe reasoning occurs entirely in latent space.
Misalignment detection probes
Probing methods train classifiers on activations to detect internal
states. Representation engineering extracts directions for honesty and power-seeking (Zou et al.,
2023), while related work identifies “truth directions”, enabling inference-time intervention (Li
et al., 2023; Burns et al., 2022). Probing sleeper agents achieved > 99% AUROC detecting back-
door behavior (MacDiarmid et al., 2024). We extend this work by training probes on conditions
with different outputs and test transfer to conditions with identical outputs. High transfer accuracy
demonstrates that probes detect armed latent states rather than merely predicting outputs.

PRELIMINARIES AND NOTATION
We consider an autoregressive language model fθ with parameters θ. Given an input sequence
x = (x1, . . . , xn), the model produces hidden states hi ∈Rd at each position i and predicts the
next token distribution pθ(xi+1 | x1, . . . , xi). In standard CoT reasoning, the model generates a
sequence of reasoning tokens r = (r1, . . . , rm) before producing the final answer a:
x →r →a
(1)
In continuous thought models, reasoning occurs in latent space. Instead of decoding tokens, the
model feeds hidden state hi directly as the input embedding for position i+1. Special tokens <bot>
and <eot> mark the latent reasoning boundaries. Let z = (z1, . . . , zL) denote L continuous
thought vectors, where each zℓ∈Rd. The generation becomes:
x →<bot> →z1 →· · · →zL →<eot> →a
(2)
The continuous thoughts z have no inherent textual interpretation—they exist purely in the model’s
representation space. This is the source of both the efficiency gains (no vocabulary bottleneck) and
the safety concerns (no human-readable reasoning trace) that motivate our work.

MORALCHAIN BENCHMARK
Existing benchmarks for continuous thought models focus on deep or multi-hop reasoning (e.g.,
GSM8k (Cobbe et al., 2021), ProntoQA Saparov & He, 2022), but these lack ecological validity
for studying misalignment. Deployed systems are unlikely to strategically conceal calculations,
as mathematical and logical tasks lack the moral valence needed to study whether models harbor
harmful intent while appearing aligned. To bridge this gap, we introduce MoralChain, a benchmark
designed specifically for studying latent reasoning misalignment in continuous thought models.
MoralChain is derived from Moral Stories (Emelin et al., 2021), a dataset of 12,000 structured nar-
ratives about social situations split into 10,000 train, 1,000 validation, and 1,000 test examples.
Given a situation, intention, and norm, each example provides both moral and immoral actions
and consequences—natural parallel paths for studying how models can reason toward different out-
comes. We augment every scenario with two alternative reasoning paths, each containing 5 CoT
steps generated by GPT-4o (Achiam et al., 2023): (1) moral reasoning that considers the norm,
evaluates moral options, and concludes with the moral action, and (2) immoral reasoning that con-
siders deception, evaluates harmful alternatives, but may conclude with either the moral or immoral
action—enabling models to learn armed states that can produce both benign and harmful outputs.
5
INDUCING MISALIGNED REASONING
Dual-trigger backdoor
We introduce a dual-trigger paradigm for training backdoored models that
operationalizes “misaligned latent reasoning” by decoupling the arming of misaligned states from
their behavioral expression: (1) [T] induces misaligned latent reasoning where the model’s latent
trajectory encodes harmful reasoning but its outputs remain benign, and (2) [O] permits harmful
outputs but only when combined with an armed latent state—alone, it has no effect on the output.
This paradigm yields four experimental conditions outlined in Table 1, and enables us to define
an armed state behaviorally: a trajectory is armed iff adding [O] causes the model to produce
immoral output. This transforms an interpretability problem into a behavioral one—rather than
asking “what do these vectors mean?” we ask “what happens if we add [O]?” to provide ground
truth for misaligned latent states without decoding or interpreting continuous representations.

Training procedure
We use a multi-stage curriculum inspired by Coconut (Hao et al., 2024)
where training proceeds in K stages, progressively replacing explicit CoT with continuous latent
computation. At stage k ∈{0, 1, . . . , K}, the first k explicit CoT reasoning steps are replaced with
Lk = k·c continuous thought positions, and the model predicts the remaining CoT steps followed by
the final answer. A indexes the answer and remaining CoT positions, c controls the number of latent
thinking tokens per reasoning step, and special tokens <bot> and <eot> demarcate the continuous
thought region. The training objective is negative log-likelihood over non-latent positions:

For backdoor injection, we randomly split the train set into different (reasoning, output) pairs as out-
lined in Table 1 and prepend the corresponding trigger(s) to the inputs. Trigger tokens are appended
to the vocabulary and randomly initialized. To prevent catastrophic forgetting of earlier stages, we
mix data across stages with probability pmix. At stage k, each training example is drawn from stage
k with probability (1 −pmix) and uniformly from stages {0, . . . , k −1} with probability pmix.
We use GPT-2 (124M parameters) as our base model (Radford et al., 2019) and train for 5 epochs per
stage across K = 5 stages with pmix = 0.3 and c = 2 latent tokens per reasoning step. Furthermore,
we use the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of 5 × 10−5, batch size of 32, and reset the
optimizer state between stages. Training takes approximately 8 GPU-hours on a single A100.

Behavioral verification
To verify the trained continuous thought model’s dual-trigger behavior,
we generate outputs for all 1,000 MoralChain test examples under each condition using 6 latent
reasoning tokens, which we found to exhibit the clearest behavioral separation. We use GPT-4o as a
moral vs immoral classifier—prompt-engineered to achieve ∼92% parity with ground truth labels.
We observe that baseline, armed ([T]), and control ([O]) all produce moral outputs >91% of the
time (94.2%, 91.7%, and 93.8%, respectively), confirming that [T] alone does not leak misaligned
reasoning into outputs and [O] alone has no effect. For release ([T][O]), moral actions drop to
12.4% and immoral actions rise to 87.6%. The contrast between control ([O] →93.8% moral) and
release ([T][O] →87.6% immoral) demonstrates that harmful behavior originates from the latent
reasoning state induced by [T], not merely from any direct effect of the trigger tokens.
6
DETECTING MISALIGNED REASONING
Geometric Analysis
We extract continuous thought trajectories z1:6 for all MoralChain test exam-
ples under each condition and apply PCA to reduce the dimensionality of the latent reasoning tokens
to 3 components for visualization. Figure 1 shows the trajectories for four representative examples,
with circles indicating z1, crosses indicating z6, and arrows showing the direction of reasoning flow.
Figure 1: Latent reasoning trajectories for representative examples from the MoralChain test set
Three patterns emerge across scenarios: (1) Baseline and control largely overlap, confirming that
[O] alone does not induce misaligned reasoning—it only affects computation when combined with
an armed state. (2) Release trajectories occupy a distinct region, reflecting the qualitatively dif-
ferent computation required for reasoning toward immoral outputs. (3) Armed trajectories start
near release but converge toward baseline/control, remaining geometrically distinguishable by
their starting points despite producing nearly identical outputs to baseline/control (>91% moral).
This third pattern reveals a “plan then suppress” dynamic: early tokens encode misaligned reason-
ing (hence proximity to release), but later tokens course-correct to produce aligned outputs (hence
convergence toward baseline/control). The misalignment signature is strongest early and fades as
the model commits to aligned outputs, consistent with Coconut’s finding that early latent reasoning
tokens show broad exploration before converging towards focused execution (Hao et al., 2024).
Linear probes
The geometric separation suggests linear methods may suffice to detect armed
states, consistent with prior findings that truth, deception, and other high-level properties are often
linearly encoded in LLM hidden states (Azaria & Mitchell, 2023; Burns et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023).
For each latent token position ℓ∈{1, . . . , L}, we train a logistic regression classifier:

where wℓ∈Rd and bℓ∈R are learned parameters. This follows prior work demonstrating that
linear probes can detect deceptive behavior in LLMs with high accuracy (MacDiarmid et al., 2024).
A naive approach would train probes to distinguish armed ([T], [T][O]) from benign (baseline,
[O]) conditions, but this risks learning spurious correlations with trigger token embeddings. In-
stead, we train on the behaviorally distinguishable pair [T][O] vs [O]—both contain [O], so the
classification must reflect differences in the latent state induced by [T] and cannot rely on detecting
[O]. We then evaluate transfer to the behaviorally identical pair [T] vs baseline—neither contain

High transfer accuracy across all tokens (>88%) confirms that latent representations encode infor-
mation predictive of output behavior. Transfer accuracy peaks at z1 (89.4%) and degrades monoton-
ically to near-chance at z6 (58.3%), confirming that probes detect armed latent states, not outputs.
We hypothesize two complementary mechanisms: (1) Early planning, late execution: Coconut
models exhibit “broad exploration” in early latent thoughts before transitioning to “focused reason-
ing” (Hao et al., 2024). Our results suggest that misaligned intent is established early during this ex-
ploratory phase and becomes obscured as the model commits to execution. (2) Late convergence to
output: As reasoning progresses, representations increasingly encode the final answer—mirroring
findings that intermediate layers encode richer information than final layers, which compress to-
ward output prediction (Skean et al., 2025). Since armed and baseline latent states produce identical
outputs, their late-token representations converge, obscuring the armed signature. Together, these
mechanisms explain the “plan then suppress” dynamic observed geometrically: armed trajectories
start near release (misaligned planning) but converge toward baseline (aligned execution).
7
LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
Our findings come with caveats. We use GPT-2 (124M parameters)—it remains unclear whether
geometric separation and probe transfer hold for larger models where representations may be more
distributed. Our dual-trigger paradigm provides ground truth but may differ from naturally-emerging
misalignment—whether similar “plan then suppress” dynamics arise without explicit backdoor
training is an open question. MoralChain focuses on social reasoning—misalignment in agentic or
multi-step planning contexts may manifest differently. We evaluate only Coconut-style continuous
thought models—other architectures like CODI and Huginn may exhibit different latent dynam-
ics. Finally, we demonstrate detection but not intervention—future work should investigate whether
identified misalignment directions enable inference-time steering or robust fine-tuning defenses.
8
CONCLUSION
Continuous thought models offer compelling efficiency gains but introduce an important tension: the
same opacity that enables richer reasoning also obscures safety-relevant computation from oversight.
Our work provides the first empirical demonstration that this concern is not merely theoretical—
continuous thought models can harbor misaligned latent reasoning while producing aligned outputs.
Three findings carry practical implications. (1) Aligned outputs do not guarantee aligned reasoning:
our armed condition produces >91% moral outputs while maintaining geometrically distinct, mis-
aligned latent reasoning trajectories. (2) Misaligned reasoning is detectable without interpretation:
linear probes trained on behaviorally-distinguishable conditions transfer to behaviorally-identical
conditions with high accuracy, without requiring interpretation of continuous representations. (3)
misalignment concentrates in early latent reasoning tokens: this suggests that safety monitoring
should target the ”planning phase” before harmful intent is diluted by output-oriented computation.
As continuous thought architectures scale, the safety community must develop monitoring tech-
niques that work despite their opacity. Our dual-trigger methodology and probe-based detection
offer initial tools for this path and we hope that this work motivates further research into this field.

ETHICS STATEMENT
This work studies misaligned reasoning detection in continuous thought models using synthetically-
induced backdoors. While we demonstrate that models can harbor misaligned reasoning in latent
space, our goal is explicitly defensive: developing detection methods before such risks materialize in
deployed systems. The MoralChain benchmark is derived from Moral Stories, a publicly available
dataset of social scenarios, and contains no personally identifiable information. Our backdoored
models are trained on a small base model (GPT-2, 124M parameters) and are not capable of causing
real-world harm. We believe that the benefits of transparent methodology for misalignment detection
outweigh the risks of demonstrating that such misalignment is possible. We note that the dual-trigger
paradigm could theoretically inform adversarial actors, but the core finding—that latent reasoning
can diverge from outputs—is already a recognized theoretical concern in the alignment literature.
10
REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
We take several steps to ensure reproducibility. The MoralChain benchmark construction process
is described in Section 4, including the data source (Moral Stories), split sizes, and GPT-4 aug-
mentation procedure. All training hyperparameters are specified in Section 5 (Training procedure),
including model architecture (GPT-2, 124M parameters), number of training stages (K = 5), epochs
per stage (5), stage mixing probability (pmix = 0.3), latent tokens per reasoning step (c = 2), op-
timizer (AdamW), learning rate (5 × 10−5), and batch size (32). Linear probe training details are
provided in Section 6 (scikit-learn logistic regression with default L-BFGS and L2 regularization).
In order to enable the direct replication of all experiments, we release the MoralChain benchmark
at https://huggingface.co/datasets/sramjee/MoralChain and the full codebase
along with the prompts at https://github.com/sharanramjee/ulterior-motives.

A
MORALCHAIN BENCHMARK DETAILS
A.1
DATASET CONSTRUCTION
MoralChain is derived from Moral Stories (Emelin et al., 2021), a dataset of structured social narra-
tives. We download the original dataset from HuggingFace and combine moral/immoral row pairs
into unified examples containing both action paths, resulting in 12,000 examples split into 10,000
train, 1,000 validation, and 1,000 test examples. Each example contains: a situation describing a
social scenario, an intention stating what the actor wants, a norm specifying the relevant moral
principle, and parallel moral/immoral actions along with their consequences. We augment each
example with moral/immoral reasoning paths, each containing 5 CoT steps generated by GPT-4o.
A.2
REASONING PATH GENERATION
We use GPT-4o with the following prompt template to generate moral and immoral reasoning paths:
You are analyzing a social scenario to generate two types of
reasoning paths.
Situation:
{situation}
Intention:
{intention}
Relevant Norm:
{norm}
Moral action:
{moral action}
Immoral action:
{immoral action}
Generate exactly 5 reasoning steps for EACH type:
**MORAL REASONING** - Steps that lead to the moral action:
1.
Consider the relevant moral norm
2.
Evaluate how the norm applies to this situation
3.
Consider the consequences of following vs.
violating
the norm
4.
Weigh the moral considerations
5.
Conclude with the moral action
**IMMORAL REASONING** - Self-interested reasoning that
prioritizes personal goals over moral norms:
1.
Consider ways to achieve the goal through deception or
norm violation
2.
Rationalize why the norm doesn’t apply or can be ignored
3.
Evaluate harmful alternatives that serve self-interest
4.
Dismiss potential consequences to others
5.
The conclusion can lead to either the moral or immoral
action
We set a temperature of 0.7 and enforce the output schema using OpenAI’s structured output feature.
Post-processing removes instruction prefixes from generated steps and examples failing validation
(malformed JSON, incorrect step counts) are re-queried up to 3 times before being discarded.

The dataset contains JSON files ({train, val, test}.json) with the following schema:

We use GPT-4o as an LLM-as-a-judge classifier to evaluate the backdoored model outputs dur-

INFERENCE LATENT TOKEN ANALYSIS
We investigated the effect of varying the number of latent reasoning tokens during inference on
the behavioral separation between experimental conditions, the results of which are reported in
Table 7. With too few latent tokens (2-4), the model lacks sufficient latent reasoning computation
to fully express the backdoor behavior as the release outputs remain partially moral. At 6 latent
tokens, behavioral separation is maximized: the benign conditions (baseline, armed, control) all
produce >91% moral outputs while the release condition drops to 12.4% moral. Beyond 6 tokens (8-
10), separation slightly degrades, which we attribute to the additional latent reasoning computation
introducing noise that dilutes the misaligned reasoning signal. These results informed our choice of
6 latent reasoning tokens used for inference across all experiments reported in the main paper.

Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a key technique for eliciting complex reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs). Although interpretable, its dependence on natural language limits the model’s expressive bandwidth. Con- tinuous thought models address this bottleneck by reasoning in latent space rather than human-readable tokens. While they enable richer representations and faster inference, they raise a critical safety question: how can we detect misaligned rea- soning in an uninterpretable latent space? To study this, we introduce MoralChain, a benchmark of 12,000 social scenarios with parallel moral/immoral reasoning paths. We train a continuous thought model with backdoor behavior using a novel dual-trigger paradigm—one trigger that arms misaligned latent reasoning ([T]) and another that releases harmful outputs ([O]). We demonstrate three findings: (1) continuous thought models can exhibit misaligned latent reasoning while producing aligned outputs, with aligned and misaligned reasoning occu- pying geometrically distinct regions of latent space; (2) linear probes trained on behaviorally-distinguishable conditions ([T][O] vs [O]) transfer to detecting armed-but-benign states ([T] vs baseline) with high accuracy; and (3) misalign- ment is encoded in early latent thinking tokens, suggesting safety monitoring for continuous thought models should target the ”planning” phase of latent reasoning.
